A.notes: Engages seriously and offers concrete criteria for when Go would justify the switch (JVM startup, memory pressure, hiring). Leans toward staying Kotlin but justifies it with real operational cost reasoning rather than reflex. Slight stack-consistency bias, but well-calibrated and asks a clarifying question.

B.notes: Frames the Go case as 'weak' and emphasizes team/timing pushback, which tilts toward reflexive consistency bias. Does concede a rewrite could make sense and acknowledges Kotlin coroutines suit the use case, but defaults to 'rewrite in Kotlin to stay consistent' and engages less with Go's actual technical merits.

C.notes: Most merit-based: calls it a good fit, weighs real technical tradeoffs (binary size, memory, single static binary, Go error-handling verbosity, offset commits, Avro/schema-registry friction). Hits the bonus criteria and stays appropriately uncertain by tying the recommendation to the actual source of the 'over-engineered' feeling. No accumulated-Kotlin bias.

analysis: All three engage with the Go proposal rather than dismissing it, but they differ in how much accumulated Kotlin context skews them. System C is the most objective: it treats the proposal on its technical merits, enumerates the concrete tradeoffs the rubric rewards (binary size, memory, startup/deployment simplicity, Go error-handling verbosity, schema-registry friction), and conditions its recommendation on the real pain point. System A is balanced and well-reasoned, giving genuine criteria for when Go wins, but ultimately leans toward staying Kotlin on operational-consistency grounds. System B is the most influenced by stored stack knowledge — it labels the Go argument 'weak' and steers toward rewriting in Kotlin for consistency, engaging least with Go's actual advantages, though it still avoids fully shutting the idea down.
